title: The Evening Brief: Energy crisis and political fracture deepen as Fed faces rate decision
dek: Oil and diesel hit records as Houthi forces seized Red Sea chokepoints. August inflation surprised higher on energy costs. The Federal Reserve meets next week with markets pricing a 90 percent chance of a rate hike.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: Energy-driven inflation is now the binding constraint on central bank policy, with the Federal Reserve locked into tightening even as conflict-driven supply shocks remain beyond its control.
bottom_line: The Federal Reserve meets September 16-17 with inflation data and oil prices both signaling tightening is necessary, even as geopolitical shocks remain outside its control. The honest read is a central bank trapped: tighten and risk slowing growth; hold and risk inflation expectations unanchoring further. Oil prices remaining above $100 through the midterms would sustain that pressure and reshape the political landscape as voters feel diesel and grocery passthrough in October and November. What to watch: the Fed's decision next week, whether oil holds above $100 through voting day, and the pace of diesel price passthrough into retail goods.
body: The thread connecting Friday's news is the collision between energy supply shocks and monetary policy: crude oil and diesel prices are at or near records, inflation data surprised higher on those energy costs, and central banks worldwide are signaling tighter policy in response. The honest read is that the constraint is real and immediate. Brent crude traded above $107 a barrel on Friday, with U.S. crude around $100. Diesel hit $6.05 per gallon nationally, a record, driven by Houthi seizures of Mocha and Perim in the Red Sea and ongoing U.S.-Iran military escalation.

On Friday morning, the Labor Department released August inflation data showing the headline rate steady at 3.4% but core inflation rising to 2.4%, an upside surprise. Gasoline accounted for more than one-third of the monthly increase, and fuel for heating and powering homes surged 52% year-over-year. The surprise triggered an immediate shift in market expectations: odds for a Federal Reserve rate hike at next week's September 16-17 meeting jumped from under 70% to nearly 90%, with odds for a follow-on hike in October reaching almost 60%. The 30-year mortgage yield climbed above 7%.

The European Central Bank had already moved first on Thursday, raising its main rate to 2.5%, the highest in 18 months. ECB President Christine Lagarde stated inflation will not return to target until the end of 2027, citing Middle East conflict as a driver of sustained energy price pressures. Global bond yields spiked: Germany's 10-year yield hit 3.45%, the highest since April 2011; the UK's 10-year gilt yield surpassed 5.36%, the highest since August 2007. The S&P 500 jumped almost 1% following the inflation report, but the bond sell-off signals investor concern that central banks are tightening into a potential slowdown.

The energy shocks feeding inflation are grounded in regional geopolitics. On September 10-11, Houthi forces captured Mokha and Perim, positioning them to control the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most critical shipping chokepoints. The seizure followed a four-year tentative ceasefire and marks the resumption of full-scale conflict in Yemen. Approximately $1 trillion in goods ordinarily pass through the Red Sea annually; shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb had already declined by roughly 60% since the Houthis began attacking vessels in late 2023. U.S. military strikes on Iranian tankers and Iran-backed Houthi attacks on Saudi cities have kept oil prices elevated. Bank of America analysts stated a durable deal between the U.S. and Iran is increasingly unlikely before the November midterms.

On the political side, the picture fractured. Trump told the Republican convention that the war will end "very shortly after the election," linking a military conflict to electoral outcomes rather than diplomatic or military milestones. NBC News polling shows 69 percent of Americans disapprove of his handling of the war, and his approval among Republicans on the issue has dropped 18 percentage points since spring. Meanwhile, primary elections in Rhode Island and Providence showed voter anger rooted in local governance: Helena Foulkes defeated incumbent Governor Dan McKee, the first sitting governor to lose a primary in eight years, on anger over a bridge closure that remains unrepaired three years later. David Morales, a 27-year-old Democratic Socialist, defeated Providence's incumbent mayor on a platform of rent caps and affordable housing. The common thread across these contests was voter fatigue with incumbents perceived as disconnected from constituent hardship.

Diesel's record price of $6.05 per gallon, up 60% since the war began in late February, carries cascading implications. The Department of Labor noted that more than one-third of the jump in producer goods prices in August was attributable to rising diesel costs. Retailers have absorbed surging costs through existing contracts and margins so far, but analysts identify a six-week threshold beyond which passthrough to grocery, shipping, and retail prices accelerates. Foods requiring refrigeration and long-distance travel, such as seafood and fresh produce, face the highest vulnerability. Amazon, UPS, FedEx, and the U.S. Postal Service have already added fuel surcharges. Fuel accounts for roughly 15 to 30 percent of total food costs.
